```text
English precision       96%
Armenian precision      78%
short Armenian pages    61%
```

If the project exists specifically to improve Armenian data, the overall number is not sufficient.

Stratify the audit along dimensions that matter to the corpus objective.

#### 9.3 Document-weighted and token-weighted quality

Suppose bad retained documents are mostly very short. Document precision can be 90% while 98% of retained **tokens** come from good documents.

Conversely, a few very long bad documents can make token-level contamination much worse than document precision suggests.

Report both when the distinction matters:

$$
P_{\mathrm{doc}}
=\frac{\#\text{good retained docs}}
{\#\text{retained docs}},
$$

and

$$
P_{\mathrm{token}}
=\frac{\text{tokens in good retained docs}}
{\text{tokens in retained docs}}.
$$

Neither replaces the other.

#### Stop and reason {#precision-recall-question}

You manually inspect 100 retained documents and 95 are good.

**Question:** Can you conclude that the filter has 95% recall?

No. A representative sample suggests that about 95% of the kept documents are good. It does not tell us how many good documents the filter discarded. That second question requires inspecting the rejected set too.

<span id="precision-recall-readable-example"></span>**A clean kept set can still lose most of the useful material.** Consider a constructed pool of 1,000 pages whose quality labels are all known:

| Filter decision | Good pages | Junk pages | Total |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Kept | 95 | 5 | 100 |
| Discarded | 405 | 495 | 900 |
| Total | 500 | 500 | 1,000 |

Looking only at the kept row, 95 of 100 pages are good: **95% precision**. Looking at all good pages, only 95 of the original 500 survived: **19% recall**. The other 405 good pages were discarded.

The denominators answer different questions: precision asks “How clean is what we kept?”; recall asks “How much of the good material did we recover?” These exact toy counts are not inferred from the preceding sample. An audit of accepted pages alone cannot reveal the missing 405.

### 10. Threshold selection is a decision under constraints {#threshold-decision}

A continuous filter score becomes a policy only after choosing a threshold.

Suppose a held-out development audit gives the following constructed results:

| Threshold | Retained docs | Precision | Recall | Armenian science retained |
| --------: | ------------: | --------: | -----: | ------------------------: |
|      0.30 |         8,500 |      0.78 |   0.96 |                       92% |
|      0.50 |         6,700 |      0.88 |   0.89 |                       81% |
|      0.65 |         5,400 |      0.93 |   0.80 |                       69% |
|      0.80 |         3,900 |      0.97 |   0.61 |                       42% |

There is no universally correct row.

A project with strict storage limits may prefer a higher threshold. A low-resource corpus may accept somewhat lower precision to preserve rare coverage. A safety-sensitive source may have non-negotiable rejection criteria separate from generic quality scoring.

The threshold choice should state the objective.

For example:

> Among policies with estimated retained precision at least 90%, choose the threshold retaining the largest number of Armenian scientific documents, subject to no protected-source violations.

This is an explicit decision rule. It can be challenged and reproduced.

#### 10.1 Precision–recall and retention curves

Always examine the curve rather than only the selected point.

Useful plots/tables include:

```text
threshold → precision
threshold → recall
threshold → documents retained
threshold → tokens retained
threshold → retention by language/source/register
```

A threshold that looks harmless globally can sharply reduce one low-resource stratum.

#### 10.2 Per-language thresholds can be justified {#language-specific-thresholds}

A single threshold assumes score meaning is sufficiently comparable across languages.

That may fail because:

* classifier calibration differs;
* document-length distributions differ;
* punctuation and segmentation patterns differ;
* available training data differ; and
* the positive class itself may have been defined unevenly.

FineWeb2 is a useful real example of a multilingual web pipeline that tunes filtering thresholds and stopword configurations by language rather than treating one global threshold as sacred.

Per-language thresholds are not automatically fair or correct. They simply make the policy explicit and allow language-specific validation.

#### 10.3 Threshold overfitting

If you try 100 thresholds and repeatedly inspect the same evaluation sample until the result looks good, that sample is now development evidence.

Keep an untouched audit set or use a nested design.

The same principle applies if you repeatedly train proxy language models to pick the best filter. Once a benchmark has guided your filter choices, it no longer serves as untouched final evidence.

---

## Part IV: Audit how processing changes the corpus {#audit-corpus-changes}

A filter makes decisions about individual documents, but its accumulated effects change the corpus. Track which sources and languages survive, inspect the text behind suspicious statistics, and use reference comparisons to investigate shifts in coverage.

### 11. Measure how the pipeline changed the corpus

A filter can improve average document cleanliness while quietly changing language, register, source, topic, and length distributions.

A corpus audit therefore asks not only:

> “How many documents survived?”

but also:

> “Which documents survived?”

#### 11.1 Before/after composition for the running example {#source-retention-example}

Suppose the 10,000-document pilot changes as follows:

| Source family                | Before docs | After docs | Document retention | Before tokens | After tokens |
| ---------------------------- | ----------: | ---------: | -----------------: | ------------: | -----------: |
| Natural Armenian web/news    |       3,000 |      2,550 |                85% |          3.6M |         3.2M |
| Armenian educational/science |       5,000 |      3,000 |                60% |          4.0M |         2.9M |
| Translated STEM              |       2,000 |      1,900 |                95% |          1.2M |        1.15M |
| **Total**                    |  **10,000** |  **7,450** |          **74.5%** |      **8.8M** |    **7.25M** |

Globally, 74.5% of documents survive.

But the policy removed 40% of the educational/science documents and only 5% of translated STEM.

If our objective was to increase **native Armenian technical coverage**, that asymmetry demands investigation.

Possible explanations include:

* native technical pages are shorter;
* formulas make them look less prose-like;
* PDF extraction is worse than structured dataset extraction;
* language identification confidence is lower on pages with Latin symbols;
* the quality model prefers the style of translated benchmark-like data.

The table does not tell us which explanation is true. It tells us where to look.

#### 11.2 Conditional versus cumulative retention {#conditional-cumulative-retention}

Suppose the web branch has:

```text
90% pass extraction integrity
85% of those pass language policy
75% of those pass quality policy
```

Cumulative retention is

$$
0.90\times0.85\times0.75
=0.57375.
$$

So only about 57.4% of the original web candidates survive all three stages.

Do not report the three percentages as though each refers to the original population.

A good stage report contains both:

```text
conditional retention at stage
cumulative retention from starting population
```

#### 11.3 Document-weighted versus token-weighted feature rates {#document-token-weighting}

Let $c_i$ be occurrences of a feature in document $i$ and $n_i$ its length.

Document-weighted mean rate:

$$
\bar r_{\mathrm{doc}}
=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^{M}\frac{c_i}{n_i}.
$$

Token-weighted corpus rate:

$$
r_{\mathrm{token}}
=\frac{\sum_i c_i}{\sum_i n_i}.
$$

Consider two documents:

```text
Doc A: 100 tokens, 10 occurrences
Doc B: 900 tokens, 0 occurrences
```

Then

$$
\bar r_{\mathrm{doc}}
=\frac{0.10+0}{2}=0.05,
$$

while

$$
r_{\mathrm{token}}
=\frac{10}{1000}=0.01.
$$

Neither is wrong.

The first asks about a uniformly selected document. The second asks about a uniformly selected token position in the corpus.

Use the weighting that matches the claim.

#### 11.4 Length distributions

Mean length can hide heavy tails. Report quantiles:

```text
p10, p25, median, p75, p90, p99
```

before and after filtering, preferably by important source/language strata.

A minimum-length filter may barely change total token count while deleting thousands of short conversational or definition-like documents.

#### 11.5 Frequency and dispersion {#frequency-and-dispersion}

A feature that appears 1,000 times can be distributed across the corpus or concentrated in one source.

Let $f_i(w)$ be the count of feature $w$ in partition $i$. Its range is

$$
\operatorname{range}(w)
=\sum_i \mathbf 1[f_i(w)>0].
$$

A simple size-adjusted dispersion statistic is

$$
DP(w)
=
\frac12\sum_i
\left|
\frac{f_i(w)}{f(w)}
-
\frac{n_i}{\sum_j n_j}
\right|,
$$

for $f(w)>0$.

If the feature distribution exactly follows corpus size, $DP=0$. Increasing concentration pushes the measure upward.

The partition matters. Document-level dispersion and source-level dispersion answer different questions.

A phrase appearing in 100 different pages from one mirrored site is widespread by page count but concentrated by source family.

Lecture 5 will connect this to duplicate and contamination structure.

### 12. Contextual inspection: statistics should lead back to text

Aggregate diagnostics are most useful when the student can return to concrete examples.

The corpus-linguistics materials emphasize concordancing—keyword-in-context (KWIC)—because a frequency is often ambiguous until we see the contexts that produced it.

For corpus engineering, the same technique can expose processing failures.

#### 12.1 Useful diagnostic queries

Search extracted text for:

```text
replacement character: �
repeated navigation: "Home | About | Contact"
boilerplate phrases
broken equation markers
very long symbol runs
HTML entity remnants
OCR artifacts
unexpected English phrases inside Armenian pages
```

Then inspect:

```text
left context | match | right context
```

sorted by source, extractor, or decision status.

A repeated footer phrase appearing in 40,000 documents may explain both a keyword spike and later false duplicate matches.

#### 12.2 Inspect accepted and rejected examples

For every high-impact filter, maintain a review view containing:

```text
raw source link/locator
extracted text
feature values
classifier scores
rule that fired
final policy decision
```

Then inspect both:

```text
high-scoring accepted documents
borderline accepted documents
borderline rejected documents
extreme rejected documents
```

The borderline cases are especially informative about threshold semantics.

#### 12.3 Exploration and prevalence estimation are different {#exploration-and-prevalence}

Handpicking suspicious examples is excellent for discovering a bug.

It is not a random sample.

Use two different workflows:

```text
exploratory inspection -> discover failure modes
probability audit       -> estimate how common they are
```

Do not report the fraction of failures in a deliberately difficult error set as corpus prevalence.

#### Stop and reason

You search rejected documents for `F = ma` and find many correct Armenian physics explanations.

**Question:** Have you estimated how often the filter wrongly removes technical material?

No. You have discovered a failure mode. To estimate prevalence, design an audit sample from the relevant rejected population.

### 13. Optional reference-based corpus comparisons

Sometimes a before/after comparison reveals which lexical or structural features a filter disproportionately removes.

A simple descriptive ratio for feature $w$ is

$$
R(w)
=
\frac{f_{\mathrm{after}}(w)/N_{\mathrm{after}}}
{f_{\mathrm{before}}(w)/N_{\mathrm{before}}}.
$$

Values below 1 indicate lower normalized prevalence after filtering; values above 1 indicate higher prevalence.

For rare features, use a documented smoothing rule before taking logarithms.

#### 13.1 Keyness-style comparisons

If students use a likelihood-ratio statistic, construct the full contingency table:

|                  | Corpus A | Corpus B |
| ---------------- | -------: | -------: |
| feature $w$      |      $a$ |      $b$ |
| all other tokens |  $N_A-a$ |  $N_B-b$ |

Expected counts are

$$
E_{ij}
=\frac{O_{i\cdot}O_{\cdot j}}
{O_{\cdot\cdot}},
$$

and

$$
G^2
=2\sum_{i,j}
O_{ij}\ln\frac{O_{ij}}{E_{ij}}.
$$

But be careful about interpretation.

Before/after corpora are **not independent samples**: one is derived from the other. Tokens within a document are also dependent, and testing thousands of features creates a multiple-comparisons problem.

Therefore, in this course, use keyness primarily as an **exploratory ranking tool** unless you have a defensible sampling/inference design.

For stronger uncertainty estimates, resample documents or source families and recompute the descriptive statistic. A bootstrap can quantify variation under the resampling scheme, but it does not repair bias in the underlying acquisition frame.

## Part V: Assemble, test, and defend the pipeline {#assemble-and-test-the-pipeline}

The final part brings these decisions together in an executable, auditable process. Compare stage order and cost, follow one document through the full pipeline, and distinguish corpus-audit evidence from evidence of model improvement. The extended practical checkpoint offers a way to apply the ideas independently.

### 14. Pipeline order changes both cost and sometimes the result

A corpus pipeline is not merely a set of filters. Order matters.

#### 14.1 Cheap filters before expensive filters {#filter-order-cost}

Start with **100 pages** and two fixed checks on the same unchanged text. A structural check detects empty or corrupted pages and costs **1 unit per page**. A neural quality scorer costs **20 units per page**. Once either check rejects a page, processing stops.

In this constructed example, 70 pages pass the structural check when it runs first, and 60 pass the neural scorer when it runs first:

| Order | First stage | Second stage | Total work |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| Structural check → neural scorer | Check 100 pages: 100 units | Score 70 survivors: 1,400 units | 1,500 units |
| Neural scorer → structural check | Score 100 pages: 2,000 units | Check 60 survivors: 60 units | 2,060 units |

Cheap-first avoids neural scoring on 30 obvious failures. Expensive-first instead pays for all 100 neural scores, saving only 40 cheap checks. The first order saves **560 units** while preserving the same final set, because both unchanged rules must pass in either order.

These are illustrative costs, not measured runtimes. Measure actual per-page cost and rejection rates before choosing an order. If a stage changes the representation or depends on an earlier stage's output, the same-final-set claim no longer follows; section 14.2 examines that case.

The general cost calculation is:

Suppose filter A costs $c_A$ per document and passes fraction $p_A$. Filter B costs $c_B$.

If A runs first, expected cost per starting document is

$$
C_{A\to B}=c_A+p_Ac_B.
$$

If B runs first,

$$
C_{B\to A}=c_B+p_Bc_A.
$$

This calculation helps schedule fixed predicates.

Example:

```text
cheap structural check:
  cost = 1 unit
  pass = 0.70

expensive neural scorer:
  cost = 20 units
  pass = 0.60
```

Cheap first:

$$
1+0.70(20)=15.
$$

Expensive first:

$$
20+0.60(1)=20.6.
$$

The cheap-first order saves computation under these assumptions.

This is **not** an independence assumption; it is an expected scheduling calculation using measured pass rates.

#### 14.2 Some transformations do not commute {#transformation-order}

If two predicates inspect the exact same immutable representation, their final intersection may be order-independent.

But many corpus operations change the representation.

Examples:

```text
normalize -> language ID
```

can differ from

```text
language ID -> normalize
```

if normalization repairs or damages characters used by the classifier.

Similarly, deduplication in Lecture 5 can interact with quality filtering. If a duplicate cluster contains one broken extraction and one clean extraction, “choose representative first, then quality-filter” can produce a different result from “score cluster members, then choose a representative.”

Do not assume pipeline stages commute because they all eventually return Booleans.

#### 14.3 Keep a transformation ledger

For every derived document, record something like:

```json
{
  "document_id": "doc-001",
  "parent_object_id": "sha256:...",
  "transformations": [
    {"run": "extract-v2", "status": "ok"},
    {"run": "normalize-nfc-v1", "status": "ok"},
    {"run": "lid-glotlid-X", "status": "ok"},
    {"run": "quality-signals-v4", "status": "ok"},
    {"run": "policy-v3", "status": "accepted"}
  ]
}
```

This makes a later question such as

> “Which documents were rejected only because of quality rule `R17`?”

answerable without reconstructing the entire pipeline from logs.

### 15. End-to-end worked trace for one document {#document-processing-trace}

Let us follow one Armenian educational page from Lecture 3 through the pipeline.

#### 15.1 Acquired object

Lecture 3 recorded:

```json
{
  "record_id": "armenian-edu:rev42:article-9182",
  "content_sha256": "abc123...",
  "mime": "text/html",
  "url": "https://example-education.am/physics/newton-2",
  "capture_time": "2026-02-14T08:31:04Z"
}
```

#### 15.2 Extraction

Extractor `html-maintext-v2` emits:

```text
heading: Նյուտոնի երկրորդ օրենքը
paragraph: ...
equation: F = ma
paragraph: ...
```

and reports:

```json
{
  "raw_chars": 18241,
  "retained_chars": 6118,
  "block_count": 9,
  "link_text_chars": 103,
  "status": "ok"
}
```

#### 15.3 Normalization

`normalize-nfc-v1` changes 6 canonically equivalent sequences and line endings but preserves block count and equation text.

Recorded evidence:

```json
{
  "unicode_form": "NFC",
  "changed_codepoint_positions": 6,
  "code_blocks_modified": 0,
  "equation_blocks_modified": 0
}
```

#### 15.4 Language evidence

Block-level LID produces:

```text
heading       hy   0.98
paragraph 1   hy   0.97
equation      und  n/a
paragraph 2   hy   0.95
references    en   0.88
```

Document policy labels it `mostly_hy`, not “invalid mixed-language.”

#### 15.5 Quality signals

```json
{
  "repeated_line_ratio": 0.00,
  "alphabetic_char_ratio": 0.74,
  "replacement_char_ratio": 0.00,
  "neural_quality_score": 0.66,
  "content_blocks": 9
}
```

The neural score is below a hypothetical global threshold of 0.70.

#### 15.6 Human audit

The auditor marks:

```json
{
  "extract_integrity": 2,
  "substantive_body": 1,
  "language": "hy",
  "technical_structure": "preserved",
  "notes": "clear school-level physics explanation"
}
```

The document becomes a **false negative** under the global threshold.

Further analysis shows many native Armenian technical pages have scores in the 0.55–0.70 range because formulas, shorter paragraphs, and source style differ from the filter's positive training examples.

This one document does not establish prevalence. It identifies a hypothesis:

> The global quality threshold may disproportionately reject native Armenian technical content.

We then test that hypothesis on a probability sample from the relevant rejected stratum.

#### 15.7 Revised policy

After held-out validation, suppose policy `v4` uses:

```text
source/language-aware threshold
+ minimum extraction-integrity rule
+ explicit preservation of technical blocks
```

The record is accepted under `v4`.

Crucially, we can explain **why** the outcome changed without re-acquiring the page.

That is what a versioned processing pipeline should enable.

### 16. Practical checkpoint: compare two defensible processing policies {#processing-policy-lab}

Use the frozen acquired inventory from Lecture 3. Work on a bounded subset large enough to contain meaningful variation but small enough to audit carefully.

The task is not “build the cleanest corpus.” The task is:

> **Compare two explicit processing policies and provide evidence for the one you would take forward.**

#### Part A — Write the document contract

Define:

* document unit;
* supported input format(s);
* block types;
* what is considered main content;
* how titles, captions, equations, code, and tables are treated;
* normalization policy;
* language label space; and
* final disposition states.

Do this **before** comparing extractors.

#### Part B — Build two extraction variants

For example:

```text
Policy A: simple DOM baseline
Policy B: stronger main-content extractor
```

or

```text
Policy A: prose-only flattening
Policy B: structure-preserving blocks
```

Run both on the same objects.

#### Part C — Construct an extraction reference sample

Create a small stratified sample across at least:

```text
source × format × document-length group
```

Annotate required blocks and order. Report extraction precision/recall and structural preservation by block type.

Do not hide failed objects from the denominator.

#### Part D — Audit language identification

Create an independent LID audit sample containing:

* ordinary Armenian prose;
* short Armenian pages;
* mixed Armenian–English text;
* code/math-heavy pages; and
* likely confusable/non-target records.

Report confusion tables and false-positive/false-negative examples. Do not report only global accuracy.

#### Part E — Define a quality rubric

Use at least three independent dimensions. Have two people annotate a shared subset without seeing the filter score if practical.

Report:

* label prevalence;
* raw agreement;
* disagreement examples;
* an agreement statistic if appropriate; and
* the adjudication rule.

#### Part F — Evaluate thresholds

On development data, produce a table/curve of:

```text
threshold
retained documents
retained tokens
estimated precision
estimated recall
retention by source/language
```

State the decision rule used to select the threshold.

Then evaluate the chosen policy once on the held-out audit set.

#### Part G — Compare the corpus before and after

At minimum report:

* documents and tokens by source;
* documents and tokens by language/origin;
* document-length quantiles;
* conditional and cumulative retention per pipeline stage;
* one dispersion/concentration diagnostic; and
* contextual examples explaining at least two observed shifts.

#### Part H — Failure portfolio

Include at least five concrete failures, such as:

```text
boilerplate retained
article body dropped
PDF reading order wrong
mixed-language page misclassified
short valid explanation rejected
formula corrupted by normalization
quality model strongly prefers one source style
```

For each, identify the responsible stage and whether the failure is detectable automatically.

#### Deliverable

Submit:

1. processing specification;
2. executable pipeline/configuration;
3. extraction reference annotations;
4. LID and quality audit annotations;
5. threshold-development report;
6. held-out audit results;
7. before/after corpus audit;
8. failure portfolio; and
9. a one-page decision memo stating which policy you would carry into Lecture 5 and what remains uncertain.


> <span id="corpus-model-evidence"></span>**Do not claim model improvement in this assignment.**
> A corpus can look cleaner under the defined audit while producing no downstream gain—or even hurting a capability. Model-level effects require controlled training experiments later in the course.

### Check your understanding

1. Why is removing HTML tags insufficient to define the main content of a web page?
2. Two extractors retain the same fraction of reference tokens. What additional evidence might still make one clearly preferable for scientific text?
3. Why can NFC normalization be a reasonable general-text choice while NFKC still requires separate justification?
4. Why does idempotence fail to establish that a normalizer is safe?
5. What is the difference between a language label from page metadata, a script detector, and a language-ID model prediction?
6. Why can a classifier with a 1% false-positive rate return mostly false positives for a rare target language?
7. What property is a classifier actually learning when its positive examples are Wikipedia and its negatives are random web pages?
8. Why is a manual audit of only retained documents insufficient to estimate filter recall?
9. When can document-weighted and token-weighted quality estimates differ substantially?
10. Why should threshold selection be reported as a decision rule rather than only as a number such as `0.7`?
11. A filter improves overall precision while reducing native Armenian science retention from 90% to 40%. What questions should you ask before adopting it?
12. Why are handpicked failure cases useful but unsuitable for estimating population prevalence?
13. Under what conditions does ordering a cheap filter before an expensive filter reduce expected cost without changing the final set?
14. Give an example of two processing stages whose order can change the final result.
15. What evidence should be retained so that a rejected document can later be reconsidered under a new policy?

### What to remember {#lecture-takeaways}

1. **Extraction defines the document.** Raw bytes do not contain a privileged “training text” waiting to be revealed.
2. **Preserve structure before flattening.** Technical information can disappear even when prose looks clean.
3. **Evaluate extraction against explicit reference content and ordering.** Length and visual plausibility are not enough.
4. **Normalization is a versioned transformation, not cosmetic cleanup.** Test preservation as well as idempotence.
5. **Language identification is a classifier.** Scores, scripts, metadata, and human labels are different evidence sources.
6. **There is no universal scalar called quality.** Define the property before training or thresholding a filter.
7. **Audit rejected material as well as retained material.** Otherwise you cannot estimate how much useful data the filter destroys.
8. **A threshold changes the corpus distribution.** Measure retention by language, source, origin, register, length, and relevant coverage dimensions.
9. **Statistics should lead back to examples.** Contextual inspection explains what aggregate shifts actually mean.
10. **The output of Lecture 4 is an audited candidate corpus, not the final training corpus.** Deduplication, contamination, and privacy are still ahead.

### References and reading

#### Core pretraining-data references

**Common Crawl.** *Get Started.* Official overview of WARC, WAT, and WET representations and data access.
https://commoncrawl.org/get-started

**Penedo, G., et al. (2024).** *The FineWeb Datasets: Decanting the Web for the Finest Text Data at Scale.* FineWeb provides a documented example of extraction, language filtering, heuristic quality filtering, deduplication, and data-ablation experiments for web pretraining data.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17557
https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceFW/fineweb

**Penedo, G., et al. (2025).** *FineWeb2: One Pipeline to Scale Them All—Adapting Pre-Training Data Processing to Every Language.* Particularly relevant for language–script labels, language-specific filtering, multilingual failure modes, and the risks of applying one global processing policy to many languages.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20920
https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceFW/fineweb-2

**Li, J., et al. (2024).** *DataComp-LM: In Search of the Next Generation of Training Sets.* Provides a controlled framework for comparing data-curation strategies through downstream language-model training rather than assuming corpus-level proxies are sufficient.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11794

#### Language identification and normalization

**Kargaran, A. H., Imani, A., Yvon, F., & Schuetze, H. (2023).** *GlotLID: Language Identification for Low-Resource Languages.* Findings of EMNLP 2023. Discusses low-resource LID, noisy metadata, closely related languages, and variety-level challenges.
https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-emnlp.410/

**Kargaran, A. H., Yvon, F., & Schuetze, H. (2024).** *MaskLID: Code-Switching Language Identification through Iterative Masking.* ACL 2024 Short Papers. Useful for understanding why a single dominant sentence-level label can hide multilingual content.
https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-short.43/

**The Unicode Consortium.** *Unicode Standard Annex #15: Unicode Normalization Forms.* Normative definitions of NFC, NFD, NFKC, and NFKD and their stability/idempotence properties.
https://unicode.org/reports/tr15/

#### Corpus-design and audit ideas adapted from the supplied materials

The lecture also adapts several ideas from the supplied corpus-linguistics teaching materials:

* **Corpus Design and Compilation:** sampling frames, representativeness, and documented corpus construction;
* **Tokenization, POS-Tagging, and Annotation:** annotation as an explicit, fallible layer and the importance of disagreement analysis;
* **Frequency, Zipf's Law, and Keyness:** normalized comparison and the need to state denominators/reference corpora;
* **Concordancing and Collocation:** returning from aggregate counts to inspectable contexts;
* **N-grams and Lexical Bundles:** frequency versus dispersion and the danger of imported thresholds;
* **Register, Genre, and Language Variation:** per-document variation and confounding;
* **Statistics for Corpus Linguistics:** observation units, effect sizes, dependence, and multiple comparisons; and
* **Arkhangelskiy's corpus-compilation workshop:** treating corpus text, metadata, annotation, and searchability as linked parts of an inspectable resource.

These corpus-linguistics methods are used here as **diagnostic tools for pretraining-data engineering**, not as a claim that a linguistic reference corpus and a language-model training corpus should have the same design or sampling proportions.
